findings.title: Non-atomic read-modify-write of match_count loses increments and writes during validation
findings.body: `should_block?` loads the record, does `record.match_count += 1` in Ruby and then `record.save`. Two concurrent signups using the same blocked address read the same `match_count` and both write the same incremented value, so increments are silently lost. It also issues an UPDATE of the whole row (including `updated_at`) from inside a read-only predicate. Use an atomic SQL update (e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...")` or `increment!`) so the statistic is correct under concurrency.

findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is exact/case-sensitive, so the block is trivially bypassed
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs an exact string comparison. Nothing in this model (or in `User.new_from_params`, which assigns `params[:email]` verbatim) normalizes case or strips whitespace, and the unique index added in the migration is on the raw column. An admin blocking `spammer@example.com` will not block a signup with `Spammer@Example.com`, and blocking `Spammer@Example.com` will not block the lowercase form. Downcase/strip the email both when persisting a BlockedEmail and when looking it up (consistent with `Email.downcase` used elsewhere).

findings.title: Validator performs a database write, so match statistics are double counted and can be rolled back
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` mutates and saves the BlockedEmail row, and it is invoked from `validate_each`. `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` (for the Discourse Hub check) and then `user.save`, so validation runs twice for a single signup attempt and `match_count` is incremented twice. Worse, the increment that happens during `save` runs inside the user's save transaction, so it is rolled back if the insert fails, while the increment from the earlier `valid?` persists — making the counter and `last_match_at` unreliable. Move the side effect out of validation (e.g. record the match in the controller/flow after the check) or make the counter update happen outside the AR transaction.

findings.title: rejectedEmails array is declared on the class and shared/never reset
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` puts a single mutable array on the controller's prototype, so every instance of `CreateAccountController` shares the same array object and `pushObject` mutates shared state. In addition the list is never cleared, so an email rejected once stays flagged as invalid for the lifetime of the page even if the server-side reason no longer applies (e.g. the whitelist setting changed, or the user corrects an unrelated field and retries). Initialize it per-instance (in `init`) and clear it when the modal is opened.

findings.title: Any email error from the server is reported to the user as "invalid"
findings.body: Every server-side email error (already-taken address, domain whitelist/blacklist rejection, blocked email) causes the email to be pushed into `rejectedEmails`, and `emailValidation` then renders the generic `user.email.invalid` reason. The actual server message (which is only shown transiently in the flash) is discarded, so users retyping the form see a misleading "invalid email" message for reasons such as "email already registered". Consider storing the server reason alongside the rejected email and displaying it.

findings.title: No coverage for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved out of User, nor for the model wiring
findings.body: The whitelist/blacklist validation was moved from `User#email_validator` into this new `EmailValidator`, but the only specs added stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and exercise the blocked branch. There is no test for `email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` behaviour in its new home, no test that an existing error on `:email` short-circuits the blocked check (the `record.errors[attribute].blank?` guard), and no test that `User` actually rejects a blocked email end-to-end via `validates :email, email: true`. A regression in the moved code or in the model wiring would go unnoticed.
